extracted.intended_audience: educators, curriculum designers, education researchers, and media literacy practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts core media-literacy skill criteria (play, simulation, performance, appropriation) used to evaluate or design learning activities that leverage participatory culture and new media. Focuses on what those skills are, why they matter, and concrete classroom/program examples and cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play
rubrics_metrics.description: Play as a mode of engagement that motivates learning and develops skills. (Includes Pratt’s account that play activities produced three kinds of learning: practicing discrete skills with clear academic payoffs; providing scaffolds that motivate and shape acquisition of other school knowledge; and developing a sense of oneself as a learner.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points and examples: • Play shifts emphasis from mere fun to deep engagement —focused, hardworking attention that can also be experienced as enjoyable (Scott Osterweil quote). • Play often requires grind and practice (not always immediate mirth) but is deeply motivated by personally meaningful goals. • Play lowers emotional stakes of failure, encouraging risk-taking and learning through trial-and-error (die and do over). • Play encourages scientific/problem-solving processes: identifying conditions, posing hypotheses, testing/refining models, applying learned solutions to new contexts; meta-gaming enables reflection and articulation of learning (Kurt Squire/Civilization III example). • Classroom suggestions (What Might Be Done): encourage free-form experimentation (alternative history scenarios), hands-on design problems (art/design), use of educational games (e.g., Supercharged for electromagnetism) and linking game experience to explicit classroom instruction. Anti-patterns/cautions: conflating play merely with fun and failing to harness its engagement or treating it only as a hook rather than a mode of sustained learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation: The Ability to Interpret and Construct Dynamic Models of Real-World Processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulations expand capacities to represent and manipulate information, allowing experimentation with complex configurations of data and the formation/testing of hypotheses through trial-and-error. They enable modeling and discovery when users understand and can manipulate underlying assumptions and variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points and examples: • Simulations are dynamic, governed by grounding assumptions, and can reveal emergent properties useful for learning (examples: Caesar III, Railroad Tycoon, SimCity). • Benefits: more compelling representations than textbooks, motivate deeper engagement, offer first-person discovery that learners treat as their own. • Skills required: reading simulations (interpreting probabilities and model assumptions), evaluating credibility and reliability of competing models (Eric Klopfer caution), customizing and designing simulations (procedural literacy; Ian Bogost). • Classroom/program suggestions: have students manipulate existing simulations and construct their own models; use activities that bridge imaginary scenarios and real-world data (fantasy sports, stock-market class exercises); involve youth in game-design projects (OnRampArts, Urban Games Academy, Global Kids). • Advanced simulation skills: understanding ‘‘embracing co-control’’ (SimCity) and using simulations to explore complex systems (fire spread example). Anti-patterns/cautions: treating simulation outputs as unquestionable facts or as purely contrived propaganda—students must learn to analyze assumptions and weigh evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance: The Ability to Adopt Alternative Identities for the Purpose of Improvisation and Discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance and role-play (including projective identity in games) let learners assume fictive identities to explore perspectives, synthesize multiple knowledge sources, and reflect on values and choices; performance cultivates improvisation, perspective-taking, and problem-solving skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points and examples: • Gee’s concept of projective identity: fusing player and avatar to project values and treat the avatar as a project in the making; this immersion can yield pedagogical payoffs (e.g., students’ emotional reactions and critical reflections in Revolution). • Performance integrates knowledge from varied sources (game content, prior learning, life experience) to build compelling characters and insights (examples: Margaret being shot in Revolution; students writing in-character journals/films). • Role-play fosters sociolinguistic and narrative understanding (Wolf & Heath; Anne Haas Dyson), lets learners embody characters and genres to demonstrate comprehension, and supports collaborative theorizing about new worlds. • Classroom/program suggestions: Model United Nations, epistemic games that simulate professional contexts, Savannah Project (embodied lion role-play with handheld devices), MySpace-style historical profiles. • Benefits beyond content: performance emphasizes learning processes (how to learn) and life skills—improvisation, perspective-taking, and the ability to test identities. Anti-patterns/cautions: treating role-play only as a fun introduction rather than recognizing its intrinsic pedagogical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation: The Ability to Meaningfully Sample and Remix Media Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation is a learning process by which students take culture apart and put it back together—sampling, remixing, and transforming prior cultural materials to create new meaning. It recognizes that creative expression builds on existing work and conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points and examples: • Appropriation reframes creativity as engagement with traditions and prior works (Homer, Shakespeare, Sistine Chapel examples). • Sampling and remixing (digital or analog) are central forms of contemporary youth expression (fan fiction, remix culture, jazz improvisation, hip-hop sampling). • Learning through appropriation involves apprenticing with styles/techniques, trying on conventions, and deliberately violating them to generate new works. • Pedagogical implications: teachers should acknowledge and build on students’ remix practices and teach how to transform source materials meaningfully rather than merely copying. Anti-patterns/cautions: reducing appropriation to piracy or illegal copying; failing to teach the difference between unethical copying and transformative remixing that contributes to cultural meaning.
